title: First Report of the Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization p. 1

description: First page of the parliamentary committee report, which is an image of a printed book. description: Pages 2-3 of the parliamentary committee report discusses the efforts made to promote immigration to Canada in the UK and Europe, and the costs incurred by the Dominion, and summarizes the contents of the rest of the report. Lists the names of individuals who testify in support of the program and refute certain of Doyle's assertions. Concludes that the work of the agents is satisfactory. Includes beginning of the committee's interview with Mr. Lowe, Secretary of the Department of Agriculture.

title: First Report of the Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization pp. 10-11
creator: Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization; Government of Canada
description: Pages 10 and 11 contain continued testimony by Mr. Lowe, Secretary of the Department of Agriculture. On page 10, Lowe summarizes the Doyle report and its recommendations, and rejects the idea of government-operated industrial establishments to train the children because it is too similar to the workhouse model. On page 11 the prospect of further investigation is raised and dismissed as being the responsibility of Provincial governments.  Lowe reads a letter from Emma G. Barber, a supervisor at Miss Macpherson's Knowlton Home, which provides rough numbers of children in various situations, emphasizing that they are children and will need "patient training," and mentioning the challenges that the wide geography poses for visiting the children once placed.

title: First Report of the Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization pp. 12-13
creator: Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization; Government of Canada
description: Page 12 contains the conclusion of Emma G. Barber's letter, then Annie Macpherson's testimony begins and continues on page 13. Macpherson mentions that her agency had brought out 2000 children since 1870, and describes the procedures for training and caring for the children in the UK and during the journey. Macpherson details the financial arrangements, bonuses, and discounts, asserting that the special rates were declined. Macpherson outlines the supervision and visiting practices after the children were sent out, and the facilitation of communication with families in the UK, and exhibits a register of children (not included). The page ends with the note that some records were lost in a fire.

title: First Report of the Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization pp. 14-15
creator: Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization; Government of Canada
description: Continued testimony from Annie Macpherson, and colleagues Miss Bilbrough and Miss Barber, addresses the financials of the homes and estimates of the number of children who had been adopted. Macpherson asserts that the Homes are made available to children who return for whatever reason, but that the older boys who were succeeding well were asked to contribute money to aid in bringing other children to Canada. They discuss "black sheep" cases, but insist that many are successful. Senator Flint testifies about a home child who became an Attorney-At-Law, with assistance from his family. Flint describes attempts to train boys at various trades, which were not successful because they could make more money working for farmers.

description: Flint's testimony continues, explaining his lack of credence in Doyle's report, especially in mixing together the work of Macpherson with Rye. Numbers about the Knowlton home are provided by M.P. Pettes, noting that only two or three had proved incorrigible out of 280. Macpherson adds that there have only been 10 deaths out of 2000 children in five years.
